notes:
Summary: Pegasus is evaluating Redwood Dedicated for low-latency trading/alerts and market QA. Primary asks: deterministic p95/p99 latency bounds, clear measurement methodology (server vs client), throughput guarantees for 24/7 trading hours, and contractual SLA language for fallbacks and capacity bursts.

SLO alignment details discussed so far (high level):
- Requested SLOs: p50/p95/p99 for both streaming and non-streaming paths. Non-streaming (batch request/response): p95 target 120ms, p99 target 200ms. Streaming (token-by-token/interactive): client-observed p95 target 250ms, p99 target 400ms.
- Measurement definitions: customer insists on client-side end-to-end measurement (SDK timer start = request creation, end = final token received), plus server-side breakdown published by Redwood (gateway latency, model runtime, post-processing). Contract should call out which metric governs SLA credits.
- Streaming vs non-streaming: clear separation required. Streaming metrics must account for first-byte latency and per-token tail. Agreement to report first-byte p50/p95/p99 and full-response completion p50/p95/p99.
- Percentile calculation windows: rolling 1h and 24h windows for operational alerts; monthly window for SLA evaluation. Explicitly define aggregation (weighted by request count).
- Cold vs warm KV/cache: benchmarks must include cold-start scenarios and warm steady-state (protocol for eviction, synthetic prefix cache warm-up). Customer concerned about cold-start p99 spikes affecting SLA — proposing an exclusion window for planned restarts but not unplanned thrashing.
- Client vs server instrumentation: recommended approach — instrument Redwood SDK to emit client-side timings to Redwood observability (opt-in), allow sync of client and server timelines for reconciliation. Also propose using signed TTL headers so replay traffic simulates production cache hit ratios.
- Throughput & reserved GPU planning: initial sizing estimate: model variant (7B Q4/F16) requires ~8x A100-equivalent GPUs to meet 500 req/s sustained at target latencies with batching disabled for tail-sensitive routes; suggest reserve 10 GPUs with bursting pool of 4 for market open events. Redwood SE to provide derived unit economics (tokens/sec per GPU, tail trade-offs with quantization).
- SLAs & fallbacks: customer wants explicit fallback policy — if p95 exceeds threshold for 15 consecutive mins, automatic failover to a cheaper lower-latency model variant or region-level fallback; credits calculation tied to monthly rolling p95; legal wants clear remediation and runbook attachments.

Action items agreed:
- Redwood to run 48-hour soak on a dedicated pool using customer's harness and model replica (customer will provide dataset and synthetic front-door). Goal: produce server-side breakdown + client-observed E2E percentiles (first-byte & completion).
- SE to produce detailed GPU sizing spreadsheet (tokens/sec, per-GPU concurrency) and cost/ARR scenarios for reserved vs burst pools.
- Draft SLO appendix for contract that enumerates which metrics govern credits (server vs client), exclusion windows, and streaming-first-byte definition.

Customer quotes: "We need tail guarantees for market open — a single long tail burst costs real money." — Head of Platform.

Sticking points: legal/data residency; whether client-side or server-side percentiles are the authoritative SLA metric; handling cold-cache tail spikes.

References: Perf deck, SLO draft and harness in linked drive. Fireflies call IDs in linked_fireflies. Jira tickets filed for baseline run anomalies (INFR-9922).
